title: Quantum and Cryptographic Resilience
summary: A six-module programme equipping supervisors to assess firms' exposure to quantum threats, cryptographic inventories and post-quantum migration plans, and to set proportionate expectations.
intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to assess the financial sector's readiness for quantum computing: understanding the threat to public-key cryptography, challenging firms' cryptographic inventories and migration plans, and setting proportionate supervisory expectations.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors a plain-language understanding of how quantum computing threatens the cryptography that secures payments, data and digital assets, and of what a credible migration to post-quantum cryptography involves. Participants leave able to assess firms' inventories, migration plans and third-party dependencies, identify red flags and contribute to the authority's quantum readiness strategy.
sections.What It Covers: Quantum computing and the cryptographic threat, harvest now decrypt later, where cryptography sits in financial services, cryptographic inventories and risk assessment, NIST post-quantum standards, migration planning and crypto-agility, third-party dependencies, impacts on payments and crypto-assets, and supervisory expectations.
Intended Audience: Supervisors and inspectors responsible for technology, cyber and operational resilience risk
Payments, market infrastructure and digital asset specialists in supervisory and central bank functions
Policy staff and senior managers shaping the authority's cyber and quantum readiness approach
Learning Objectives: Explain how quantum computing threatens public-key cryptography and why the risk is already present
Identify where cryptography is embedded in financial services and which assets are most exposed
Assess the completeness and quality of a firm's cryptographic inventory and risk assessment
Evaluate post-quantum migration plans, crypto-agility and the use of NIST standards
Analyse third-party, payments and crypto-asset dependencies that constrain migration
Design proportionate supervisory expectations and a quantum readiness plan for the authority
sections.Structure and Format: Six modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a two-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a plain-language technical briefing with case studies and supervisory question exercises, and modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of cyber, technology risk or operational resilience supervision is helpful. No background in mathematics or cryptography is required.
Core Reading: NIST, FIPS 203, 204 and 205: Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (2024)
G7 Cyber Expert Group, Public Statement on Planning for the Opportunities and Risks of Quantum Computing (2024)

modules.title: Quantum Computing and the Cryptographic Threat
modules.summary: A plain-language introduction to quantum computing, why it breaks today's public-key cryptography, the uncertainty around timelines and why data harvested now may be decrypted later.
objectives: Explain in plain language how quantum computers differ from classical computers
Distinguish the impact of quantum attacks on public-key and symmetric cryptography
Assess the harvest now, decrypt later risk and its link to data shelf life
syllabus: Qubits, error correction and the path to cryptographically relevant machines
Why public-key encryption and digital signatures are most at risk
Timeline estimates and why uncertainty is not a reason to wait
Harvest now, decrypt later and long-lived confidential data

modules.title: Where Cryptography Sits in Financial Services
modules.summary: A map of where cryptography protects the financial system, from customer channels and payment messaging to hardware security modules, certificates and digital signatures on contracts and ledgers.
objectives: Identify the main uses of cryptography across financial services
Analyse which systems and data carry the highest quantum exposure
Explain why cryptography is often invisible and poorly documented within firms
syllabus: Secure communications, certificates and public key infrastructure
Payment cards, messaging networks and hardware security modules
Digital signatures, identity and authentication
Embedded cryptography in legacy and vendor systems

modules.title: Cryptographic Inventories and Risk Assessment
modules.summary: How firms discover and record where and how cryptography is used, prioritise exposed systems and data, and how supervisors judge whether an inventory is complete and decision-useful.
objectives: Explain the purpose and contents of a cryptographic inventory
Assess the completeness of a firm's inventory, including third-party and embedded uses
Evaluate a firm's prioritisation of systems by exposure and data shelf life
syllabus: Discovery tools, manual review and the cryptographic bill of materials
Prioritising by data sensitivity, shelf life and system criticality
Governance: ownership, board reporting and risk appetite
Red flags: partial inventories and no named owner

modules.title: Post-Quantum Standards, Migration and Crypto-Agility
modules.summary: The NIST post-quantum standards, what a realistic multi-year migration programme involves, and why crypto-agility is as important as the choice of algorithm.
objectives: Explain the NIST post-quantum cryptography standards and their intended uses
Assess the credibility, sequencing and resourcing of a firm's migration plan
Evaluate a firm's approach to crypto-agility and hybrid deployment
syllabus: NIST post-quantum standards: ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA
Migration roadmaps, milestones and testing
Hybrid schemes, performance impacts and interoperability
Crypto-agility as a design principle for future change

modules.title: Third Parties, Payments and Crypto-Assets
modules.summary: Why most firms depend on vendors, payment schemes and market infrastructures to migrate, and the particular challenges quantum computing poses for blockchains, wallets and digital asset custody.
objectives: Assess firms' reliance on vendors and infrastructures for post-quantum migration
Analyse coordination challenges in payment systems and market infrastructure
Evaluate quantum risks to blockchain signatures, wallets and custody
syllabus: Vendor roadmaps, contractual commitments and supply chain assurance
Coordinated migration across payment schemes and settlement systems
Quantum exposure of blockchain signatures and exposed public keys
Implications for crypto-asset custody and tokenised assets

modules.title: Supervisory Expectations and Quantum Readiness
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into proportionate supervisory expectations for quantum readiness, the international work under way and an action plan for the authority's own systems.
objectives: Compare emerging supervisory and international approaches to quantum readiness
Formulate proportionate supervisory expectations for different types of firm
Design a quantum readiness plan for the authority and its regulated population
syllabus: International work: BIS, G7 Cyber Expert Group and national cyber agencies
Embedding quantum risk in cyber and operational resilience supervision
The authority's own cryptographic exposure and migration
Workshop: the authority's quantum readiness action plan

related.title: Big Tech, Embedded Finance and Open Finance
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping supervisors to assess big tech, embedded finance and open finance models, and their concentration, conduct and operational risks.

related.title: Digital Operational Resilience under DORA (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on DORA for supervisors and financial entities: ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and TLPT, ICT third-party risk and critical provider oversight.

related.title: Operational Resilience, Cyber and Critical Third Parties
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess firms' operational resilience, cyber risk, incident response and third-party dependencies, and to shape the authority's resilience strategy.

related.title: Crypto and Blockchain Fundamentals
related.summary: A ten-module foundation programme giving supervisors a practical understanding of blockchain, crypto-asset markets and service providers, and the risks they must supervise.

related.title: Crypto-Asset Regulation and Supervision
related.summary: An advanced twelve-module programme equipping supervisors to authorise, supervise and take action against crypto-asset firms under comprehensive regimes and international standards.

related.title: Digital Money: Stablecoins, Tokenised Deposits and CBDCs
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and central bankers to assess stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs, and their risks to payments and financial stability.
